items.q: What layered architecture do you use? How do MVVM and MVI compare?
shortAnswer: Three layers: **UI** (Compose + state holder), **domain** (optional — use cases, pure Kotlin), and **data** (repositories + data sources). Dependencies point inward; data never touches UI.
MVVM and MVI both use unidirectional data flow. MVI goes further: **one immutable state object** plus **explicit intents** makes inconsistent states impossible.
MVVM with one `StateFlow<UiState>` is MVI-lite in practice. And that is what most modern Android codebases ship.
items.answer:
#### The layers
- **UI layer** — composables plus a state holder (`ViewModel`). Holds no business logic; renders state, forwards events.
- **Domain layer** (optional) — use cases encapsulating business rules, reusable across ViewModels; overhead for one-line pass-throughs.
- **Data layer** — repositories own the single source of truth; data sources (network, database, DataStore) sit behind them.

**Rule:** dependencies point inward (UI → domain → data); expose domain models, not DTOs.

#### Unidirectional data flow
State flows down, events flow up; the screen calls a ViewModel function that updates the single source of truth, which re-emits.

#### MVVM vs MVI
| | MVVM (common form) | MVI |
|---|---|---|
| State | often several `StateFlow`s | exactly one immutable `State` |
| Input | public ViewModel methods | a sealed `Intent`/`Action` type sent to one `dispatch` |
| Reducer | ad-hoc updates | explicit `(State, Action) -> State` |
| Wins | less boilerplate | impossible states become unrepresentable; trivially testable |
| Costs | multiple flows can drift out of sync | ceremony, and a large sealed hierarchy |

#### What to actually say
"I use MVVM with a single immutable `UiState` as one `StateFlow`, events as a sealed type — MVI's guarantee without the ceremony. I'd add a formal reducer only for a screen with complex transitions worth unit-testing."

#### Modeling state well
Prefer a sealed hierarchy or explicit flags over independent booleans; `isLoading = true` **and** `error != null` must be unrepresentable.

code.caption: Single-state ViewModel with events modeled explicitly

followUps: When is a domain layer genuinely worth the extra indirection?
How do you model one-shot events (navigation, snackbars) without the replay bug?
Why expose `StateFlow` rather than `LiveData` in a new codebase?
traps: Reciting layer names without being able to justify the domain layer. Interviewers push on 'why not call the repository directly?'
Multiple independent `StateFlow`s that can disagree — the exact bug a single state object prevents.

items.q: How do Hilt's components and scopes work? How does it compare to Koin?
shortAnswer: Hilt builds a component hierarchy that mirrors Android lifecycles: `SingletonComponent` → `ActivityComponent` → `FragmentComponent`, each with a matching scope.
Scope annotations (`@Singleton`, `@ActivityRetainedScoped`, `@ViewModelScoped`, `@ActivityScoped`) control **instance reuse**; without a scope, every injection creates a new instance.
Hilt: compile-time verified, Android-only. Koin: runtime resolution, no codegen, first-class KMP support — so KMP projects often pick it.
items.answer:
#### The component hierarchy
- `SingletonComponent` — `@Singleton` — app lifetime
- `ActivityRetainedComponent` — `@ActivityRetainedScoped` — survives config change
- `ViewModelComponent` — `@ViewModelScoped` — one ViewModel
- `ActivityComponent` — `@ActivityScoped` — one Activity instance
- `FragmentComponent` — `@FragmentScoped`
- `ViewComponent` — `@ViewScoped`

A child can inject anything its parents provide, never the reverse.

#### The pieces
- `@HiltAndroidApp` on `Application`; `@AndroidEntryPoint` on Activity/Fragment/Service; `@HiltViewModel` on ViewModels.
- `@Module @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)` declares bindings; `@Binds` for interface→implementation; `@Provides` for things you don't own (Retrofit, Room, OkHttp).
- **Qualifiers** (`@Named` or custom) when two bindings share a type — e.g. `@IoDispatcher` vs `@DefaultDispatcher`.
- **Assisted injection** (`@AssistedInject` + `@AssistedFactory`) when arguments are known only at runtime — e.g. a ViewModel id.
- `@EntryPoint` for classes Hilt doesn't own (a `ContentProvider`).

#### Hilt vs Koin in 2026
| | Hilt | Koin |
|---|---|---|
| Errors | compile time | runtime (unless using annotations+KSP) |
| Cost | KSP processing at build time | slight startup/resolve cost |
| KMP | Android only | full KMP support |
| Style | annotations | Kotlin DSL, or annotations via KSP |

Koin now has a compile-time path via KSP, narrowing the gap — recommended for larger Koin codebases or module-by-module migrations.

#### What a strong answer sounds like
"Hilt for an Android-only app — I want the graph verified at compile time. Koin for KMP, since Hilt can't cross that boundary. I inject dispatchers via qualifiers to stay testable, and I keep modules feature-organized rather than one giant `AppModule`."

code.caption: Qualifiers, @Binds, and assisted injection

followUps: What's the difference between `@Binds` and `@Provides`, and why prefer `@Binds`?
How would you structure DI modules in a 40-module app?
traps: Confusing 'scope' with 'lifetime of the object you inject'. An unscoped binding gives a **new instance every time**, which surprises people with caches and singletons.
One monolithic `AppModule` — it becomes a build bottleneck and a merge-conflict magnet.

items.q: How do you build an offline-first repository with sync and conflict resolution?
shortAnswer: **The database is the single source of truth.** The UI only ever observes the database; the network is a background process that writes into it.
Writes go into a local **outbox/mutation queue** with a pending flag, so the UI updates optimistically and a worker drains the queue with retries.
Conflicts need an explicit policy: last-write-wins with server timestamps is the default; use version vectors or CRDTs when concurrent edits must merge.
items.answer:
#### The shape
`UI ──observes──▶ Room (source of truth) ◀── Sync worker ──▶ Network`

The UI never awaits the network. `repo.observeItems()` returns a `Flow` from Room; refresh is fallible and only updates the database.

#### Reads
- Room `Flow` → UI, instant from cache; refresh fetches → upserts → the Flow re-emits.
- Track `lastSyncedAt` staleness to show "updated 2 h ago" and drive auto-refresh.
- Paged data: **Paging 3 + `RemoteMediator`** — Room is the paging source, the mediator writes fetched pages in.

#### Writes
1. Write locally with a **client-generated id** (UUID) and `pendingSync = true`, emitting immediately for an optimistic result.
2. Enqueue unique `WorkManager` work to drain the outbox.
3. Success: swap client id for server id, clear the flag. Failure: mark failed, surface retry.
4. **Idempotency keys** so a retry after an ambiguous timeout doesn't duplicate.

#### Conflict resolution
- **Last-write-wins** with a *server* timestamp — simple, silently loses data.
- **Version / ETag check** — send your version; a moved version gets 409, then auto-merge or prompt.
- **Field-level merge** — merge non-overlapping edits; needs per-field timestamps.
- **CRDTs / operational transform** — real concurrent editing (notes, docs). Expensive; justify only if needed.

#### Delta sync
Keep a server cursor/`updatedSince` token, request only changes, handle tombstones — else deleted rows persist.

#### What interviewers score
Name the database as source of truth, the outbox, idempotency, and a conflict policy **with its trade-off** — vagueness is the most common senior miss.

code.caption: Optimistic write into an outbox, drained by a worker

followUps: How do you handle deletions in a delta-sync protocol?
Why do you need a client-generated id before the server responds?
How would you show sync status honestly in the UI without being noisy?
traps: Letting the UI await the network. The moment you do, you have an online-first app with a cache, not an offline-first app.
Ignoring idempotency. Retries after timeouts are the single biggest source of duplicated records in mobile sync.

items.q: How would you modularize a large Android app? What does it buy you?
shortAnswer: Split by feature first, then by layer inside feature (`feature:search:ui`, `feature:search:data`); shared core modules hold design system, network, database, common models.
Use **api/impl separation**: modules depend on an `api` module that holds interfaces, so changing an implementation does not recompile its consumers.
The real wins are build times, enforced boundaries, and independent team ownership — not architectural purity.
items.answer:
#### A structure that works
- `app/` — assembly, DI wiring
- `feature/search/` — ui + viewmodel + its own data
- `feature/profile/`
- `core/designsystem/` — theme, components
- `core/ui/` — composables aware of domain models
- `core/data/` — repositories
- `core/network/` — Retrofit/Ktor setup
- `core/database/` — Room
- `core/model/` — pure Kotlin domain models
- `core/common/` — dispatchers, Result, utils
- `build-logic/` — convention plugins

Features never depend on each other; cross-feature navigation lives in the `app` module or a navigation contract.

#### api/impl separation
`feature:search` depends on `core:data:api` (interfaces only); `core:data:impl` is wired at `app`. Since the `api` ABI rarely changes, an edit recompiles one module, not the world.

#### Convention plugins
Don't copy-paste build files. Put shared configuration in `build-logic` precompiled plugins: `plugins { id("myapp.android.library"); id("myapp.android.library.compose") }`. Pair with a **version catalog** (`libs.versions.toml`). AGP 9 applies the Kotlin plugin itself; convention plugins no longer add `org.jetbrains.kotlin.android`.

#### What it actually buys
- **Build speed** — independent modules build in parallel; configuration cache plus build cache skip untouched modules.
- **Enforced boundaries** — you can't reach into another feature's internals; `internal` becomes meaningful.
- **Ownership** — teams own modules, CODEOWNERS works, review scope shrinks.
- **Dynamic delivery** — optional install-time or on-demand feature modules.

#### The costs to acknowledge
More Gradle files, slower configuration if done naively, DI wiring complexity, navigation abstraction. A 5-screen app should not be 30 modules.

code.caption: A convention plugin removing per-module boilerplate

followUps: How do you handle navigation between feature modules that can't see each other?
What's the downside of too many small modules?
How would you measure whether modularization actually improved build times?
traps: Modularizing by layer only (`ui`, `domain`, `data` as three modules). You get all the ceremony and almost none of the build-time benefit, because every change still touches every module.
Not being able to name a cost. 'It's just better' reads as inexperience.
